reasons.reason: When people consume a smaller share, they save more, and that extra saving gets invested and recirculated through banks, so each initial dollar of spending ends up generating a larger total effect on output.
The multiplier equals one divided by one minus the MPC, so if households spend a smaller share of each extra dollar, every round of re-spending shrinks and the multiplier gets smaller.
An undervalued currency makes the country's goods cheap for foreign buyers while making foreign goods expensive at home, so firms should sell more abroad and the country should buy less from outside.

With a weak currency, firms that rely on imported inputs face much higher costs, which cuts their purchases from abroad and also raises their production costs, leaving them less competitive and selling less overseas too.

A lower rate means banks earn less by lending reserves to each other, so they have less incentive to lend at all, and with less lending going on, fewer deposits get created and the money supply shrinks.

Raising the target rate makes reserves more expensive to borrow, so banks cut back on lending, fewer new deposits are created, and the money supply contracts, which is exactly how the central bank tightens.
A recessionary gap is literally the shortfall of output below what the economy could produce at full employment, so real output sitting under its potential level is the defining feature.
In a downturn, discouraged workers drop out of the labor force and stop being counted, so the measured unemployment rate can actually fall below its natural level while output is weak.
A surplus means the government takes in more than it pays out, and its main income is tax revenue, so collections running ahead of spending is what leaves money left over.
A surplus is about having more in real terms than you commit nominally; when real output outruns nominal output, the real tax base exceeds what the nominal budget has promised to spend.
When the currency loses value, domestic goods get cheaper for foreigners and imports get pricier at home, so exports rise relative to imports and net exports, which is the trade balance, improve.
A falling exchange rate signals a weakening economy, and exporters end up paying more for the imported parts and fuel they need, which raises their costs and cuts how much they can ship abroad.

Crowding out is about one sector's spending pushing out another's; when private investment expands and absorbs the available savings, there is less room left for government purchases, so public spending gets squeezed.
When the government borrows to fund extra spending, it competes for loanable funds and pushes interest rates up, and those higher rates discourage businesses from borrowing to invest in new capital.
If the domestic currency weakens against the euro, every euro the firm earns from European sales converts into more units of domestic currency, so its export revenue measured at home goes up.

The depreciation means the domestic currency is worth less, so whatever the firm earns, once stated in that weaker home currency, buys less than before, and its export revenue at home effectively falls.
Higher domestic interest rates attract foreign investors looking for better returns, and to buy domestic assets they need domestic currency, so demand for it rises and its value goes up.

Investors worry that higher borrowing costs will slow the domestic economy and hurt company profits, so they sell domestic stocks and move funds elsewhere, and that selling pushes the currency's value down.
When the money supply falls, money becomes scarcer and people want to hold onto more of it as a cushion, so the amount of money demanded at every interest rate goes up.
As national income rises, people make more transactions and need more cash and checking balances to carry them out, so they want to hold more money at every interest rate.
If unemployment falls, more people are earning and spending, which pushes up total spending in dollar terms, and that spending is what nominal GDP counts while the economy's real capacity stays put.
Nominal GDP values output at current prices while real GDP holds prices fixed, so if only the price level rises, the same quantity of goods gets a bigger dollar value without any real change.

The expenditures approach adds up government outlays, and transfer payments such as pensions and unemployment benefits are a big part of what the government spends, so they belong in the government component.
The expenditures approach sums consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, so spending by businesses on new capital equipment and structures is one of its four core components.
Raising the reserve requirement forces banks to hold back a larger share of deposits, so they can lend less, the money supply shrinks, and that tightening is what makes a policy contractionary.

Lowering the discount rate signals that the central bank sees weakness ahead, and banks respond by building up precautionary reserves instead of lending, which holds back credit growth and slows the economy.

With a higher reserve requirement, each deposit is backed by more reserves, so the banking system is safer and people trust it more, bringing more money into banks and letting deposits expand further.
The money multiplier is one over the reserve ratio, so a higher requirement shrinks it, and with banks able to lend out less of each deposit, the total money supply falls as well.
With fewer training programs, workers stop waiting around for retraining and take the jobs that already exist, so they spend less time between jobs and frictional unemployment drops over time.
The natural rate is mostly frictional and structural unemployment, and better job matching shortens the time people spend searching and links workers to jobs that fit their skills, lowering both.
